title: The Bodhisattva's Practice of Gratitude
speaker: Chiko Amie Diller
summary: Chiko Amie Diller's main teaching emphasizes that true gratitude goes beyond a self-help practice focused on getting something out of it, instead embracing our interconnectedness with all things and recognizing the preciousness of life as a fleeting gift. By letting go of ego and individuality, we can tap into a sense of belonging and appreciate the beauty in ourselves, others, and the world around us. This gratitude allows us to be fully present and aware, even in difficult times, and find joy and peace in every moment.

sentences.text: Do we start with the chant?
*Unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with even in 100,000 million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good morning.
Thank you so much, Chris, for that wonderful introduction.
It's wonderful to actually be here in the same virtual zendo with you after so long, and with all of you, joined warm hearts to warm hearts.
Thank you for having me here, and also thank you for your practice together.
It really is lovely to see you.
While I don't know many of you, I believe that we have sat in intimate silence together in Samish sesshin.
Often my schedule is such that I squeeze in and disappear before the end, and also often [unclear: "with every day's end as well"].
So I always enjoy actually seeing you and meeting you and having a little more interaction.
Also, I'm here in California in the Central Valley.
We've seen many images, of course, in the news, dramatic images of torrential rain and raging rivers and flooded streets up there.
So I truly hope all of you have recovered and that you and your loved ones and your communities are all doing well and are safe.
Here we are together after our Thanksgiving feasts and busyness and often complicated family gatherings, whoever you feel and consider your family to be.
During these last weeks I noticed that this word and this concept of gratitude has been bandied about like a tennis ball, to the point where it began to feel a bit cliche for me.
I've been reading about the benefits of gratitude, and hearing some talks, not all Dharma talks but other talks, on gratitude and research on gratitude.

It began to sound like yet another best-selling self-help book: practice gratitude, and you'll sleep better and you'll look 10 years younger, and your work will improve and you'll get to be a happier and better person.
Of course this isn't wrong or negative or bad.
In fact, these things are sweet and very helpful in our troubled world and our troubled hearts.
We need all the help we can get, right?
And yet, talking solely in these terms reduces this profound practice of gratitude to "what can I get out of it?"
What can we get out of it?
Then it becomes linked to being happy when things go well, and we're left unhappy when they don't.
It's like we're so thrilled and happy when we come out of COVID lockdown and then unhappy when this latest COVID variant threatens us.
This reinforces our mistaken experience that we're separate, individual selves, walking around and bumping into each other in our proverbial spacesuits with bubbles, right?

It's hard to let go of that, and then deeply savor and appreciate this one birth, life, death, as it is: the fleeting gift that the Diamond Sutra reminds us is like a flash of lightning, a star at dawn, a dew drop, a bubble, a dream.
To be clear, I'm not saying do not practice or cultivate gratitude.
There are many wonderful Zen and other Buddhist practices of gratitude.
Personally, I've noticed that the more I actively practice gratitude, cultivate gratitude, open to gratitude, choose gratitude, the more gratitude becomes a portal to a sense that we all belong.
That we all radically belong.

Embrace that all that is and all that is not, cultivating gratitude for this body, as cranky as it gets sometimes, for friends and family, as annoying as they might be sometimes, for the white clouds in the blue sky, for our practice.
Notice, all this softens into a sense of belonging.
All this softens into noticing that life is living itself through and around and with us in every moment.
Stop.
Notice.
Attend to.
Be present for.
Then these magical gifts of ordinary everyday birth, life, death reveal themselves as sacred.
There's a poem that I love from David White.
It's called "Everything Is Waiting for You."
*The great mistake is to act the drama as if you were alone.
As if life were a progressive and cunning crime with no witness to the tiny hidden transgressions.
To feel abandoned is to deny the intimacy of your surroundings.*
*Surely, even you at times have felt the grand array, the swelling presence, and the chorus crowding out your solo voice.
You must note the way the soap dish enables you, or the window latch grants you your freedom.
Alertness is the hidden discipline of familiarity.
The stairs are your mentor of things to come.
The doors have always been there to frighten you and invite you.
And the tiny speaker in the phone is your dream ladder to divinity.
Put down the weight of your aloneness and ease into the conversation.
The kettle is singing even as it pours you a drink.
The cooking pots have left their arrogant aloofness and seen the good in you at last.
All the birds and creatures of the world are unutterably themselves.*
*Everything.
Everything is waiting for you.*
This is gratitude: opening a door to the joy, the wonderment of simply being present and alive and resting in the very heart of Buddha.
Gratitude and generosity and belonging flow together.
Gratitude is like breathing in, letting our hearts, ourselves, our core be touched by the beauty and the goodness in others, in ourselves, in the world around us.
Generosity is like breathing out, sensing our mutual belonging and offering our attentive hearts to the world.
*When body and mind are at peace, all things appear as they are.
Perfect.
Complete.
Lacking nothing.* That's Dogen Zenji.
So in Buddhism, in Zen, this practice of gratitude is pervasive and profound.
We know that our practice isn't a self-improvement project.
It's not about being a better self, but about discovering and experiencing our true self, which is another thing entirely.
It's deeply accepting and becoming the totality of who we are and of who we are not.
We understand that who we are is not who we think we are or who we feel we are, or even who we perceive ourselves to be.
Our practice is simple: get out of our own way and begin to sense and taste and feel our inner being, which includes every human, animal, plant, tree, stone, the whole universe, the whole shebang.
Not coming, not going.
This is gratitude.
In zazen, letting go of all words, thoughts, grasping, rejection, not holding on to any experience at all, whether it's wonderful or awful.
This is gratitude.
Taigen Dan Leighton wrote a lovely piece, I think recently, on Dogen and his sense of devotion and gratitude.
He said, *notice that we see that Dogen developed a full meditation practice not based on accomplishing some awakened or liberation state through self power, through our own effort.
Rather, his meditation teachings are deeply involved with devotional gratitude for support from Buddhas, ancestral teachers, Bodhisattvas, and from the awakened Buddhaland itself.*
My root heart teacher Maureen Stuart Roshi used to say, "When you become completely you, Zen becomes Zen."
Now, maybe she picked this up from Suzuki Roshi.
I don't know.
Back then we didn't have the internet.
What I do know is that she completely lived gratefulness.

For those of you who don't know, by the way, Maureen Stuart Roshi was a first generation American Zen teacher, a marvelous concert pianist full of life, a student of Soen Roshi, Yamada Roshi, and Yasutani Roshi.
She was also a dear friend of Norman and Kathy Fisher and their family when the children were quite young.
Maureen Stuart Roshi was grounded in the tradition of Sanbo Kyodan, so she practiced and taught this wonderful seamless blend of Rinzai and Soto Zen in Cambridge, Massachusetts.
In around 1987, she was diagnosed with cancer, and about two years later, she passed away.
In the last days of her life I flew in to be with her in the hospital.
She was in a state where she couldn't respond to anyone directly, to questions, to statements, but a door would bang and she would say, "Thank you."
The nurse would have to start yet another IV and she would say, "Thank you."
They'd turn her over and she would say, "Thank you."
This was an amazing teaching for me, seeing her stripped completely bare of any persona, of any self-consciousness, which she had very little as far as I could tell anyway.
What flowed through was this natural expression of gratitude, spontaneously.
No "oh, I should be this way" or "this would be a kind thing to do," just flowing through her heart.
Wow.
That is gratitude.
It's one that one doesn't pick and choose.
This is an expression of gratitude big enough to embrace and express a boundless cosmos.
It's a gratitude which doesn't exclude anything.
It has nothing to do with our usual thinking of, is this good?
Is this bad?
Does it hurt?
Does it feel good?
Do I like it?
Do I not like it?
It's far beyond that.
It's the practice of fearlessly being who we are, precisely the person we naturally are, original wholeness.
So we live in very difficult times.
We know that.
So is gratitude truly big enough to embrace the climate crisis, ravaging our world?
COVID cropping up again in all its forms, just when we think we might have a breather?
Racial injustice that's revealed daily, economic uncertainty, disparity, even despair that are terrifying.
I know here in my neighborhood, in the Central Valley of California, there are homeless encampments just expanding and popping up daily as house prices and rentals go through the roof.
So we see it.
We hear about it.
We feel it.
Many of us are impacted personally.
So we might wonder, what about my own personal stance and safety in this pain and difficulty in this uncertain world?
What about my sometimes trivial personal terrible moods or grumpiness or even feelings of loss and despair, of heartbreak, of vulnerability?
Is this truly all included in gratitude?
Yes, because this gratitude isn't a denial of life's difficulties.
We know where the Dharma lotus grows: in the mud, right?
So we need this compost, as stinky as it is sometimes.
I remember Jack Kornfield talking about the prayer that was taught to him when he was in, I believe it was, the Thai forest monastery.
I've also heard this echoed both in Tibetan Buddhism very deeply and in Pali sutras.
The prayer is, *may I be given the appropriate difficulties so my heart can truly open with compassion.*
One of Maureen's favorite stories was of a woman Zen teacher who was heard wailing and wailing after the death of a beloved grandchild.
The villagers looked at each other, confused, and finally one of them went up to the teacher and said, "You are a great Zen teacher.
You teach on death and impermanence.
What are you doing weeping and wailing?"
"Yes," she said.
"I am a Zen teacher, and I am also a grandmother."
Nothing excluded.
This is gratitude.
Recently, I was walking by the river by our house.
The American River is a very short distance away.
As I was walking, a young man, whom I'd never seen down there before, jumped onto the trail in front of me.
He was blocking my way, and he was short and wiry and very angry and probably maybe jacked up on meth or something.
I don't know.
His face was inches from my face, raging, yelling, and I tried speaking to him softly.
He got more angry, and so I tried moving out of the way and that pissed him off.
So I turned and walked the other way and he jumped around in front of me.
For a moment, I thought, I don't know if he has a knife or a weapon.
But even if he didn't, he was young and buff and strong, and I was helpless and powerless.
I suddenly realized that, as much as we practice and I practice with "life is impermanent, death is certain, death can come at any time," here it was.
This was very possibly it.
In that moment, in that second, I looked up and the tree leaves sparkled in the sunlight more brightly.
The river sang more sweetly.
The blue sky glowed with a very deep, rich vibrancy.
In that moment, which I felt might truly be my last, the world was exquisitely, vividly, ferociously alive.
The world was in me and life was living itself through me, even through my terrified heart beating very loudly in my ears, and tears of love flowing for life, for my family.
Gratitude for each precious second.
In this very moment, joy broke through.
Gratitude for life as it is, for death as it is.
And obviously I'm still here.
Dog walkers came around the corner, the guy took off, and so I'm in this world for another moment anyway.
I thought about how Eugene O'Neill described it: *For a moment I lost myself, actually lost my life.
I was set free, I dissolved in the high dim starry sky.

I belonged without past or future, within peace and unity and a wild joy, within something greater than my own life.* One of his poems, Allen Ginsberg sings, *under the burden of solitude, under the burden of dissatisfaction, the weight, the weight we carry is love.*
Maureen Stuart Roshi once said, "Yes, yes, yes.
Say yes to it, whatever life it is.
If pain comes, let it come.
If joy comes, let it come.
Neither approving nor rejecting, whatever it is, this is gratitude.
This is zazen.
This is our practice."
This is love.
We have Buddhas and ancestors.
We have cranberries.
We have wild women and men who dedicate their lives to keeping our lineages alive.

We have beautiful, I don't know about up there, down here, we have these beautiful, I think they're called Chinese pistachios or something like this, vivid, vivid, vivid crimson leaves, now raining down on us.
We pay homage to them all.
We pay homage to the Buddhas before Buddha, to the Bodhisattvas.
And this is gratitude.
So Suzuki Roshi said, *everything is Buddha's activity.
Whatever you do, or even if you keep from doing something, Buddha is in that activity.
Because people have no such understanding of Buddha, they think that what they do is the most important thing without knowing who it is that is actually doing it.
People think they are doing various things, but actually Buddha is doing everything.
You are not sitting zazen.
Zazen is sitting you.*
So I think that is all I have to say this morning.
Thank you very, very much.
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to be calm.*
